The discussion highlights critical issues—public safety, healthcare access, and economic development—facing the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe. However, federal audits reveal systemic failures: the Indian Health Service remains underfunded despite $1.8 billion in Bipartisan Infrastructure Law allocations, with 800+ projects lagging.

Meanwhile, the Laken Riley Act (H.R. 7511) mandates detention for criminal illegal aliens, yet ICE's 2025 enforcement data shows only 17% of targeted operations met processing benchmarks. Economic promises clash with reality—Tribal unemployment persists at 8.9%, triple the national rate.

Until D.C. prioritizes efficient spending over performative politics, Tribal nations will face empty rhetoric, not real progress.

The "Right Drug Dose Now Act of 2025" aligns with this push for tech-driven healthcare reform. By integrating pharmacogenomic testing into EHR systems (Section 5), it addresses the core issue: bureaucratic inefficiency in drug safety. Adverse drug events cost taxpayers $3.5B annually—AI-driven diagnostics and genetic testing could slash that waste while personalizing care.

RFK Jr’s HHS partnership with Apple/Google on wearables (Fox 7/30) proves the admin’s commitment to dismantling legacy systems that hoard data. But real success requires forcing EHR vendors to adopt open standards—not just voluntary pledges. The bill’s mandate for drug-gene interaction alerts (Sec 5(b)) is key.

Patients deserve control, not clipboards. Now audit the $40B EHR industry’s compliance costs.
